findings.text: The implementation maintains one processor information record per CPU plus a separate boot processor snapshot. Secondary CPUs refresh their own record and reconcile against the boot snapshot, while boot initialization fills CPU zero then copies it as the baseline for later feature handling.

Instruction cache policy is derived from the cache type register of the current CPU. Only the private-cache policy leaves global cache flags untouched; all other encodings set the aliasing indicator. The detected policy label and CPU number are reported once per sampling.

A dense table indexed by kernel capability number provides the short user-visible name for each 64-bit hardware capability, covering floating point, vector, cryptography, atomic, reliability, virtualization and the scalable vector and matrix extension families. The table order is defined by the capability index constants and drives feature listing output.

Two smaller tables indexed by derived log indices provide short names for 32-bit compatibility capabilities. Several legacy positions are intentionally empty because those extensions cannot occur on this architecture, while the second table covers newer compatibility extensions.

The per-CPU information view iterates over online processors using sequence iteration callbacks. Each entry reports the logical number, an emulated speed value derived from loop calibration, a feature word list, and implementation, variant, part and revision identity extracted from the MIDR, with an extra model line for 32-bit personalities.

Feature listing depends on personality. Native tasks enumerate the 64-bit capability table filtered by global feature state. Compatibility tasks enumerate the two 32-bit tables filtered by compatibility masks, skipping empty slots after a one-time diagnostic.

Each CPU owns a register object under its device node. The identification group exposes three identity registers, and when matrix extension support is present a second identification group exposes the matrix feature register. Attribute reads render as hexadecimal when the main identity is present and produce no output otherwise.

Registration initializes one empty object per possible CPU then installs dynamic online and offline callbacks. Online handling attaches the register object to the CPU device and creates the identification group, merging the matrix group when supported. Offline handling removes the group and detaches the object only if previously attached.

Collection samples timer frequency, cache type, cache maintenance, main identity, revision, auxiliary, debug, instruction-set, memory-model, floating and vector extension registers, with conditional handling for hypervisor, legacy 32-bit and matrix state. Boot and secondary entry points share the core sampler but differ in baseline handling.

One power-management identifier is deliberately not sampled during generic collection to avoid faults under firmware or override conditions and is deferred to feature code. Matrix priority subfields are masked out on read, and cache type uses an effective value that accounts for cross-CPU topology rather than the raw register.

Old-memory access maps a single physical page with write-back attributes, copies a caller-sized slice at a given offset into an iterator, then releases the mapping and reports the copied length, with zero-length requests completing immediately. Header access copies from the linear mapping and advances the supplied position.

The monitor architecture level is obtained by extracting the debug version field from the sanitized debug feature register. Monitor control state is read and written through dedicated wrappers around the control system register.

A global flag defaults to enabled, is published through a debug filesystem boolean, and can be cleared by an early boot parameter. The monitor enable path programs hardware only when the flag remains set.

Two per-CPU counters track monitor and kernel-debug enable requests. The first monitor request arms the monitor bit and the first kernel request while targeting kernel level arms the kernel bit; the last matching release clears the corresponding bit. Callers must run in non-preemptible context.

A per-CPU starting hook clears both operating-system lock registers then issues an ordering barrier. Initialization registers this hook as a dedicated architecture hotplug step with no offline action.

Single-step state in saved program status is managed by set and clear helpers plus a macro alias for task registers. A rewind helper sets the bit when the thread single-step flag is active so return resumes in the active rather than pending stepping state.

User trap delivery operates only on user-mode contexts, warns otherwise, enables interrupts when the saved state allows, then forces a trap signal with trace semantics at the current instruction address for a user-mode debug event.

User-level step exceptions are first offered to the uprobe step handler and, if unclaimed, deliver a trace trap to the task followed by a rewind. Kernel-level step exceptions are first offered to the debugger step handler when armed and, if unclaimed, emit a warning and re-arm stepping before return.

Kernel breakpoint exceptions are classified by comment or encoding and dispatched in fixed precedence to handlers for compiler-inserted traps, control-flow integrity, reserved faults, sanitizers, debugger breakpoints and dynamic probes, returning unhandled when no classifier matches.

The uprobe step path checks that the resumed address matches the expected out-of-line location advanced by one instruction, warning on mismatch, then delegates to the post-step notifier to decide whether the event is claimed.

No explicit mutex, spinlock or memory-ordering primitive appears in these fragments. Isolation relies on per-CPU records and counters, read-mostly global tables and flags, and the serialization provided by hotplug callbacks and sequence iteration.
